doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Living the music: Eddie Condon's scene, Chicago and band camp
summary: Influences from 52nd Street records, his father's collection, Danny Seraphine of Chicago and his teaching at a band camp.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah. I know exactly what you mean. They seem to have — maybe it’s just the lives they’ve led.
Maria Schneider said something about that. She said, “you have to live a life if you want to” — you can’t just play music you have to —

You have to live it. That’s right. And that’s true for any music. Look at the rock & rollers. They live it. Why don’t the jazzers? Well they did. For a long time. I think back, I was heavily influenced by the 52nd Street Eddie Condon’s and Jimmy Ryan’s and that whole scene there in the 50s. Hugely influenced. I just bought all the records I could. My dad had a lot in his collection too. He wasn’t so much of a big band guy, I started the big band collection. Dad had Ray Charles records and Oscar Peterson Trio and Sergio Mendes. That was how I practiced my bossa novas. Sergio Mendes and Brazil ’66. And I still listen to it ‘til this day. But then the rock thing for me too, I practiced and practiced and practiced to the band Chicago. I loved that band Chicago. And Danny Seraphine, the original drummer. I’ve recently gotten in touch with him. I teach at a band camp two weeks out of the year near Sacramento. It’s a traditional jazz camp. We don’t read any music other than lead sheets. So it’s all improvised. And the teachers will play and say, here’s the role of the clarinet, here’s the role of the tenor, here’s the role of the trumpet. And try and teach the kids how to play music totally improvising. Like jazz groups do. Pick a tune and play. So we’re there. And I had a student who has become my number one fan. He has a show in California called “Percussion Discussion.” And it’s an NPR show. It’s just in California now. And he interviews all kinds of drummers. So Danny Seraphine, the original drummer from Chicago, who disappeared for a long time, I never knew where he went. He had a falling out with the band and just took his money and went. He has now reappeared on the scene and wrote a book about his experience with Chicago and growing up as a tough kid in Chicago. And Jim got an autographed copy of that book to me. And I was like wow. Because I had told him Danny Seraphine was a huge influence on me on the rock thing. Playing with rock bands, like with horns. Chicago; Blood, Sweat & Tears; Earth, Wind & Fire; the Tower of Power; all the funk bands. All the rock bands. But Chicago was my most favorite. Their first record.
